vignette:
She is 20, an African woman who now works long shifts in a neighborhood pharmacy, standing under bright fluorescent lights and counting tablets with a precision that feels, to other people, like calm. By the time she tells her story, it is clear that the careful way she labels bottles and checks expiry dates is not only professionalism. It is also the way she keeps herself from drifting back to the place where time lost its order.

Before the torture, she describes herself as ambitious and fast-moving, someone who had always been proud of how much she could endure. She likes science, likes the logic of medicine, and likes being the person others come to for help. She is in a relationship now, and when she speaks about her boyfriend there is warmth, but also a watchfulness, as if closeness is something she wants and braces against at the same time.

The traumatic period begins after she is detained. She does not tell it all at once. Over several conversations, the details come in fragments, with long silences between them. She remembers a room that smells of sweat, metal, and dirty water. She remembers being tied down. She remembers voices more vividly than faces. The men who hurt her speak as if she is no longer a person but an object they can break for information, for power, for amusement. She is beaten, threatened, deprived of sleep, and made to believe repeatedly that she will die there. She learns to focus on tiny details to stay alive: a crack in the wall, the scrape of a shoe across concrete, the number of breaths she can count before pain interrupts her. At some point, fear stops feeling sharp and becomes a kind of numbness. She says that was the worst part-not only what they did, but the moment she feels herself disappear inward because feeling everything would be unbearable.

When she is finally released, the world outside is too bright, too open, and strangely unreal. People expect relief, but she does not feel free in the way they imagine. At night she cannot sleep for more than an hour or two at a time. The moment she begins to drift off, she is back in the room, hearing the same footsteps, waiting for the next blow. She wakes soaked in sweat, heart pounding, sometimes already halfway across the bedroom before she knows where she is. During the day, sudden noises make her flinch so hard that she feels embarrassed afterward. If someone comes up behind her unexpectedly, her body reacts before her mind does.

Returning to work in the pharmacy gives her structure, but it also exposes how much has changed. A customer raises his voice over a delayed prescription, and she feels heat flood her body, her hands turning cold as the shelves seem to tilt around her. The sharp antiseptic smell near the back storage area reminds her of the sour, chemical odor from detention, and for a moment she is no longer at work. She stares at a tray of blister packs without seeing them. A colleague asks if she is all right, and she says she is just tired. Tired becomes the explanation for everything.

She starts avoiding anything that might let the memories in. She skips news from home. She deletes messages she cannot bear to read. She avoids dark rooms, locked doors, arguments, even certain songs because she has learned that memory travels through strange routes. Her boyfriend notices that she keeps checking the windows and the lock, especially before bed. If he reaches for her while she is half asleep, she startles violently and sometimes pushes him away. She hates the look on his face afterward-hurt mixed with confusion-and then hates herself for having that reaction. She wants comfort but cannot stay relaxed inside it.

There are also changes she experiences as more private and harder to confess. Parts of her feel permanently altered. She used to think of herself as capable and strong; now she often feels damaged, as if something essential was taken from her in that room. She struggles with bursts of anger that seem to come from nowhere. At other times she feels nothing at all, moving through a whole day at the pharmacy with a pleasant, efficient smile while feeling hollow underneath. She tells herself she should be grateful to have survived, to have work, to have love. Instead she lives with a constant sense of danger, as if the worst thing has happened once and therefore can happen again at any moment.

Even in ordinary settings, her mind searches for exits, scans faces, measures tone. She notices who is standing near the door, whose footsteps are heavy, which men are speaking too loudly. She sits where she can see the room. Sleep remains fractured. Nightmares come in full scenes or in flashes of sensation: pressure on her wrists, breath she cannot control, a voice just outside her line of sight. In the morning she gets dressed carefully, goes to the pharmacy, and does her job well. To others she appears disciplined and mature beyond her years. Inside, she is still living as though captivity has not fully ended.
